correctness.rationale: The target exponent pattern is exactly (2,1,1,1). Write f(z)=(z+1)/(z-1), g(z)=(z²+z+1)/(z(z-1)); f,g and g/f decrease with prime z, so p=2 or 3 is too large, p>=11 too small, and p=5,7 lead to exactly five surviving (p,q) pairs. Squaring the largest prime s is impossible: reducing the full equation modulo s would force prime s to divide a product of three positive factors strictly smaller than s. For a square among the first three primes, monotone next-prime cutoffs leave exactly 21 third-prime triples, without bounding the last prime. Setting R=g(t)*f(u)*f(v) forces s=(2+R)/(2-R), and all six integral s>r are composite (559,249,63,63,32,39). The exact known witness has sigma=2822400 and phi=1411200. Independent rational arithmetic recovered five stop equalities, 21 triples and six composites. This is a global argument, not a finite search for n.
residual_risks: The proof does not exclude squarefree four-prime solutions, multiplicity >=6 beyond a known example, or other right-hand-side multipliers.
Direct integer tests through a finite bound do not establish universal exclusion; it depends on the monotone rational cutoff and congruence.
